title: Why $9.99 Works on Your Brain (Even When You Know the Trick)
description: One cent should not matter. Yet prices ending in .99 change what we buy, and in one real experiment a HIGHER price sold more. Here is the glitch in your brain behind it, the studies that proved it, and a three-second habit that switches it off.
sources: Thomas, M. & Morwitz, V. (2005). Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition. Journal of Consumer Research, 32(1).
Anderson, E. & Simester, D. (2003). Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments. Quantitative Marketing and Economics, 1(1).
Lacetera, N., Pope, D. & Sydnor, J. (2012). Heuristic Thinking and Limited Attention in the Car Market. American Economic Review, 102(5).

beats.text: This price tag is lying to you.

beats.text: One. *Cent.*
That is the whole lie. And it has been quietly working on your wallet for your entire life.

beats.text: Part one. The glitch.
Your brain is a brilliant organ. It is also, it turns out, not to be trusted with a price tag.

visual.prompt: a proud brain wearing a tiny top hat and monocle, sitting on a velvet cushion

beats.text: It reads numbers from left to right, and it makes up its mind early.

visual.prompt: a large brass magnifying glass sweeping across a sheet of cream paper

beats.text: So 2.99 starts with a two, and gets filed under two dollars and something.
beats.say: So two ninety-nine starts with a two, and gets filed under two dollars and something.

visual.prompt: a heavy iron ship anchor resting on a stack of copper coins, side view

beats.text: But look at the actual gap. It is not close to two. It is one cent away from three.
Researchers Manoj Thomas and Vicki Morwitz tested this in 2005.
beats.say: Researchers Manoj Thomas and Vicki Morwitz tested this in two thousand and five.

doc.headline: The left-digit effect in price cognition
doc.body: In a series of experiments, people judged $2.99 as noticeably cheaper than $3.00, but saw almost no difference between $3.59 and $3.60. The nine only worked its magic when the leftmost digit changed.
doc.highlight: only worked its magic when the leftmost digit changed

beats.text: In other words, the cents barely register. The first digit does almost all of the talking.
Retailers noticed. Retailers always notice.

visual.prompt: a smug shopkeeper in a striped apron rubbing his hands behind an ornate brass cash register

beats.text: Part two. The proof.
Lab tests are one thing. But the strangest result came from a real clothing catalog, with real customers spending real money.

visual.prompt: a cheerful woman in a 1950s dress opening a mail-order parcel at her front door

beats.text: Economists Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester sent out different versions of the same catalog. Same dress. Three different prices.

visual.prompt: an elegant 1950s dress displayed on a dress form in a boutique, soft spotlight

beats.text: 34 dollars. 39 dollars. And 44 dollars.
beats.say: Thirty-four dollars. Thirty-nine dollars. And forty-four dollars.

beats.text: Which one sold the most? Not the cheapest. The 39 dollar dress outsold the 34 dollar one.
beats.say: Which one sold the most? Not the cheapest. The thirty-nine dollar dress outsold the thirty-four dollar one.

visual.prompt: a shocked 1950s shop owner in an apron staring at a sales ledger, mouth wide open

beats.text: Five dollars more expensive, and more popular. The nine at the end did not just look cheaper. It looked like a deal.
And it is not only price tags. It shows up wherever there is a number on the left.

visual.prompt: a shiny 1950s sedan on a used car lot with festive bunting flags

beats.text: One study looked at more than 22 million wholesale used-car sales.
beats.say: One study looked at more than twenty-two million wholesale used-car sales.

beats.text: Prices dropped sharply every time the odometer crossed a round ten-thousand-mile mark.

beats.text: A car with 79,900 miles is the same car as one with 80,000. Buyers still paid noticeably more for it.
beats.say: A car with seventy-nine thousand nine hundred miles is the same car as one with eighty thousand. Buyers still paid noticeably more for it.

beats.text: Part three. How to switch it off.
Here is the three-second habit. Before you decide, round the price up. Out loud, if you have to.
beats.say: Here is the three-second habit. Before you decide, round the price up. Out loud, if you have to.

visual.prompt: a pencil writing a big round number on a small cream notepad

beats.text: Round. It. *Up.*
9.99 is ten. 49.99 is fifty. Say the round number, and the magic trick stops working.
beats.say: Nine ninety-nine is ten. Forty-nine ninety-nine is fifty. Say the round number, and the magic trick stops working.

visual.prompt: a disappointed vintage stage magician lifting an empty top hat under a theatrical spotlight

beats.text: And when a price ends in nine, ask one question. Is this actually cheap, or is it just dressed up as cheap?
The people who set that price know exactly how your brain reads it. Now, so do you.

beats.text: Why does every price end in ninety-nine?
Because your brain reads prices from left to right, and the first digit wins.
Two ninety-nine gets filed as two dollars. It is one cent from three.
Stores know this. That is exactly why every price ends in…

beats.text: A more expensive dress sold more. Here is how.
A real catalog printed the same dress at thirty-four, thirty-nine and forty-four dollars.
The thirty-nine dollar version beat the thirty-four.
The nine made it look like a deal, even though it cost more.
Which is how a more expensive dress sold more.
Seventy-nine thousand nine hundred miles, or eighty thousand?
Same car. But a study of over twenty-two million sales found buyers pay noticeably more for the first one.
Every round ten-thousand-mile mark, the price drops. Your brain just sees the first digit.
So, would you pay more for seventy-nine thousand nine hundred miles, or eighty thousand?
Here is a three-second trick that saves you money.
When you see nine ninety-nine, say ten. Out loud.
Forty-nine ninety-nine? Fifty. The magic stops working.
Because your brain trusts the first digit, and stores price for it. That is the whole trick.
Want it again? Here is a three-second trick that saves you money.
Your brain cannot read a price properly.
It reads left to right and decides on the first digit.
So two ninety-nine feels like two. It is one cent from three.
Researchers proved it in two thousand and five. Which is why, honestly, your brain cannot read a price properly.

shorts.title: One cent is lying to you #shorts

beats.text: One cent is lying to you right now.
Nine ninety-nine is not nine dollars. It is ten, minus a magic trick.
Stores, car dealers, streaming apps. They all use the same one-cent illusion.
Now you know. And the next time you see a price, remember, one cent is lying to you.
